## What it is

There is an asymmetry in the burden of proof. *Before* publication, a single serious flaw raised by a reviewer, such as a coding error or an unaccounted confounder, can sink a paper. *After* publication, the same flaw raised by a critic is treated as one opinion among many, and the published result keeps its standing as the default truth. The paper, like a political incumbent, has the advantage.

## Why it matters

The asymmetry makes the published record stickier than the evidence warrants. Errors that slipped through review, which is noisy (see [The problem with peer review](problem-with-peer-review.qmd)), become very hard to remove. Critics need much stronger evidence to dislodge a published claim than reviewers needed to block it. That makes post-publication criticism, the main way science corrects itself, both thankless and largely ineffective.

## How it works

A toy model. Each paper has a flaw of some severity $s$. Before publication, a reviewer notices it with some probability and rejects the paper if $s > t_{\text{pre}}$. After publication, a critic notices it and the paper is corrected only if $s > t_{\text{post}}$, where $t_{\text{post}} > t_{\text{pre}}$. Papers whose flaws fall between the two thresholds are the ones that would have been rejected but are never corrected.

## Simulated example

There are 5,000 papers with flaws of varying severity. Set the pre- and post-publication thresholds and see how many seriously flawed papers persist.

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
import {rng, range, fmt, pct} from "../js/stats.js"
```

```{ojs}
viewof tPre = Inputs.range([0.5, 3], {value: 1.5, step: 0.1, label: "Severity that blocks publication (pre)"})
viewof tPost = Inputs.range([0.5, 5], {value: 3, step: 0.1, label: "Severity needed to correct after publication (post)"})
viewof pNotice = Inputs.range([0.1, 1], {value: 0.5, step: 0.05, label: "Chance a reviewer notices a flaw"})
viewof seed = Inputs.range([1, 500], {value: 89, step: 1, label: "Random seed"})
```

```{ojs}
incumbency = {
  const r = rng(seed);
  return range(5000).map(() => {
    const s = r.exponential(0.8);
    const blocked = r() < pNotice && s > tPre;
    const corrected = !blocked && s > tPost;
    return {s, status: blocked ? "Rejected in review" : corrected ? "Corrected after publication" : (s > tPre ? "Published; serious flaw persists" : "Published; minor or no flaw")};
  });
}
```

```{ojs}
Plot.plot({
  ariaLabel: "Research Incumbency Rule: simulation chart",
  ariaDescription: "Horizontal axis: Severity of the paper's flaw. Vertical axis: Papers. The chart updates with the controls above it, and the summary below the charts states the result in words.",
  height: 280,
  x: {label: "Severity of the paper's flaw", grid: true},
  y: {label: "Papers"},
  color: {legend: true, domain: ["Published; minor or no flaw", "Rejected in review", "Published; serious flaw persists", "Corrected after publication"], range: ["#ccc", "#2166ac", "#d6604d", "#5aae61"]},
  marks: [
    Plot.rectY(incumbency, Plot.binX({y: "count"}, {x: "s", fill: "status", thresholds: 50})),
    Plot.ruleX([tPre], {stroke: "#2166ac", strokeDasharray: "4 3"}),
    Plot.ruleX([tPost], {stroke: "#5aae61", strokeDasharray: "4 3"}),
    Plot.ruleY([0])
  ]
})
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
{
  const c = k => incumbency.filter(d => d.status === k).length;
  return html`<div class="sim-readout">${md`**${c("Published; serious flaw persists")}** papers have flaws serious enough that a reviewer would have rejected them, yet they stay in the literature (red). Only **${c("Corrected after publication")}** get corrected. Lower the post-publication bar to the pre-publication bar and the red region disappears.`}</div>`;
}
```

## Key takeaways

::: takeaways
- Published results get an incumbency advantage that the evidence may not justify.
- A flaw is just as serious after publication as before.
- Apply the same standard to post-publication criticism as to pre-publication review.
:::
